Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette:
Rajesh is a 44-year-old chef who came to therapy at the urging of his sous-chef, who had grown concerned about his increasingly erratic behavior in the kitchen. Rajesh had been a respected head chef for over a decade, known for his calm precision under pressure, but in recent months he had become someone his staff barely recognized. He had come to the United States as a refugee nearly twenty years ago, fleeing a civil war that had destroyed his village and taken the lives of his parents and younger sister. What he carried with him was not a story he could tell in words—when he tried, the details dissolved into images and sensations that felt disconnected from language, as though the event belonged to someone else entirely. Sometimes he could recall the day in fragments: the sound of mortar fire, the dust rising in clouds, the weight of his sister’s hand slipping from his as he ran. But when he tried to describe it to a doctor or a friend, the words felt hollow, like reading a script about a stranger’s life. And at other times, when the memory surfaced unbidden, he was flooded with a grief so overwhelming that he would have to stop whatever he was doing and brace himself against a counter until it passed.

In the kitchen, Rajesh had always thrived on controlled chaos—the heat, the noise, the urgency of service. But now that same environment had become a minefield. The clatter of a metal tray hitting the floor could send him into a silent freeze. A delivery driver’s loud laugh from the alley made him drop a knife. What frightened him most was the way his own body responded before his mind could catch up: his heart would race, his palms would sweat, and he would find himself scanning the room for exits, counting the steps to the back door, the fire escape, the alley. He had begun to insist on prepping in a corner of the kitchen where he could see both doors, and he would become irritable if a line cook stood too close to the only exit. His concentration, once his greatest asset, had fractured; he would read a ticket three times and still forget the order, or find himself staring at a cutting board for minutes at a time, unable to remember what he was doing.

Outside of work, Rajesh’s world had shrunk. He had stopped going to the farmer’s market, which he had once loved, because the open plaza left him feeling exposed and vulnerable, as though he might be seen from too many angles. He avoided driving past the VA hospital because the sight of a uniformed officer or a parked military vehicle made his throat tighten. He had learned to change his route to the grocery store to avoid a corner where a car had rear-ended another vehicle the week before—not because the accident was serious, but because the sight of the dented bumper and the bystanders’ worried faces had triggered a flash of the dust and the screaming that he could not put into words. When a customer at the restaurant mentioned a news story about a car crash, Rajesh would excuse himself to the walk-in cooler and stand there, breathing slowly, until the urge to flee subsided.

The guilt was a constant companion. He had come to believe that he should have done more—should have pulled his sister faster, should have stayed behind, should have somehow stopped what was unstoppable. He could not forgive himself for being alive when his parents and sister were not. And he was certain that the person he had been before—the easygoing, focused chef who laughed with his staff and experimented with new recipes—was gone forever. He felt permanently broken, as though the trauma had rewritten his core. When he felt threatened, which was often, he found himself becoming overly compliant, agreeing with whatever a customer or manager said even when he disagreed, nodding along, offering apologies for things that were not his fault. It was a reflex he despised but could not control.

What finally brought Rajesh to seek help was a single moment during dinner service. A paramedic had walked into the restaurant to pick up a takeout order, and Rajesh, catching a glimpse of the uniform from the pass, had frozen mid-plate. He could not speak. He could not move. His sous-chef had to physically guide him to the office, where he sat shaking for twenty minutes. That night, Rajesh called the number his employee had given him weeks ago. He was terrified that he was losing his mind, but more than that, he was terrified of losing the only world he had left—the kitchen, his staff, the small life he had rebuilt from rubble. He did not know if he could be fixed, but he knew he could not go on as he was.
